strengths: Proposes APEX, an elegant and practical paradigm that converts virtual screening over massive combinatorial libraries into a rapid, declarative, exact top-k retrieval task using factorized neural surrogates.
Provides a custom GPU implementation using a PyTorch CUDA C++ extension and the AIR top-k algorithm, enabling the screening of 10 billion compounds in under 30 seconds on a single consumer T4 GPU.

Generates and releases a massive open-source combinatorial library benchmark (with 1M, 12M, and 10B compounds, annotated with docking scores against five medically relevant targets), which is a valuable resource for the cheminformatics and ML community.
Demonstrates strong empirical results with high recall of ground-truth top compounds, significantly outperforming Thompson Sampling under comparable evaluation budgets.
weaknesses: The accuracy of the factorized surrogate degrades for docking scores, as shown by the lower R-squared values in Figure 7 (ranging from 0.2 to 0.4). This suggests that non-additive/synergistic interactions between synthons are difficult to capture with the linear associative map, which could be discussed more extensively as a core limitation.
While the comparison with Thompson Sampling is valuable, the paper lacks experimental comparisons against other state-of-the-art CSL-specific search algorithms such as V-SYNTHES.

strengths: Addresses a highly important and computationally challenging bottleneck in drug discovery: virtual screening of ultra-large combinatorial synthesis libraries (CSLs) containing billions of compounds.

Proposes a clever and elegant methodology (APEX) that factorizes a neural surrogate's embeddings hierarchically, allowing the final property prediction to be computed as a simple sum of additive synthon contributions. This reduces the time complexity of full-library screening dramatically.
Demonstrates exceptional computational efficiency, showing that a search over a 10 billion compound library can be completed in under 30 seconds on a cheap, commodity GPU (NVIDIA T4).
Contributes a highly valuable, open-source benchmark CSL with over 10 million fully-docked and annotated compounds to foster reproducibility and future research in this area.
weaknesses: There is a noticeable drop in prediction accuracy ($R^2$) when moving from the original surrogate model to the factorized version, particularly for the docking scores (as shown in Figure 7). The authors should discuss the implications of this accuracy loss on downstream wet-lab success rates.

It is not entirely clear how the model handles unseen synthons or reactions. If the 12M/10B evaluation libraries contain synthons not present in the 1M training set, how robust is the generalization of the SynthonEncoder? If they only contain seen synthons, this limitation in generalization should be discussed.

The baseline comparison is somewhat limited. While comparison with Thompson Sampling is provided on a subset, comparing with other state-of-the-art CSL search methods (e.g., V-SYNTHES) on the full scale would make the empirical evaluation stronger.

strengths: The concept of factorizing molecular embeddings into additive synthon-level contributions is highly elegant and effectively addresses the major scalability bottleneck of virtual screening at the tera-scale.
Extremely strong empirical performance in terms of execution speed, demonstrating exhaustive screening of a 10 billion compound library in under 30 seconds on a single, affordable NVIDIA T4 GPU.
The contribution of a public, fully-annotated 12M-compound benchmark combinatorial synthesis library (CSL) is a highly valuable resource for the drug discovery and ML communities.
The methodology is mathematically clean and well-illustrated, making the paper highly accessible and reproducible.
weaknesses: The quality of the retrieval is heavily bound by the predictive accuracy of the surrogate and its factorized counterpart. As shown in Figure 7, for some targets like MET and ESR1, the R-squared values for the factorized surrogate are relatively low (below 0.4), which raises concerns about the actual biological utility of the retrieved top-k compounds for harder targets.

The baseline comparison is somewhat limited; while Thompson Sampling is a solid choice, the comparison is restricted to the unconstrained case on a subset of reactions, rather than evaluating against SOTA active learning virtual screening methods (e.g., V-SYNTHES) over the full multi-reaction library.

The manuscript lacks an explicit breakdown of the offline computational costs, specifically the time and resources needed to generate the 1M docking scores and train both the surrogate and the factorizer models.

There is limited discussion on generalization to completely unseen synthons, as the 1M training set is a downsampled version of the larger library, meaning the model likely benefits from seeing the same components during training.

strengths: Addresses a crucial bottleneck in drug discovery by enabling rapid, on-the-fly virtual screening over ultra-large combinatorial synthesis libraries (CSLs) containing tens of billions of compounds.

Presents an elegant technical approach that factorizes surrogate neural network embeddings into additive synthon-specific key-value contributions, reducing computational complexity from linear to logarithmic with respect to library size.

Provides a thorough empirical evaluation by constructing an open-source, reproducible 10-billion-compound benchmark CSL with fully docked subsets, allowing rigorous verification against ground-truth top-k sets.
Demonstrates exceptional computational efficiency, running an exhaustive search over 10 billion compounds in under 30 seconds on a single commodity Tesla T4 GPU.
Natively supports arbitrary, user-specified combinations of objectives and drug-likeness constraints at query time without requiring any model retraining or fine-tuning.
weaknesses: The linear associative factorization assumption may struggle to capture strong cooperative/non-linear interactions between synthons, as indicated by lower R-squared and recall scores for some targets (e.g., ESR1 and F10).
Comparison against other modern virtual screening baselines (such as joint protein-ligand representation models or deep active learning) is primarily qualitative rather than quantitative.
The custom BRICS-based benchmark library does not guarantee synthetic feasibility, though it remains a suitable proxy for evaluating the search algorithm's performance.

strengths: Highly impactful and practical problem: Virtual screening of ultra-large combinatorial synthesis libraries (CSLs) containing tens of billions of compounds is a key bottleneck in computer-aided drug discovery.

Clever methodology: Exploiting the hierarchical, combinatorial structure of CSLs to factorize a neural network surrogate model into additive per-synthon contributions is elegant and theoretically sound. This reduces the search complexity from linear in library size to a highly amortized lookup.

Outstanding scale of experiments: The authors build and evaluate on an open 10-billion compound library, and also test the approach on the commercial 70-billion compound Enamine REAL library in a zero-shot fashion.
Impressive performance: The custom CUDA-based top-k implementation allows screening 10B compounds in under 30 seconds on a single commodity T4 GPU.

High value to the community: The creation of a 10M+ benchmark dataset with computed docking scores and RDKit properties is a fantastic resource for reproducibility and benchmarking future CSL screening methods.
weaknesses: Compound error rates: The pipeline uses a two-stage approximation (Oracle -> Surrogate -> Factorizer). The cumulative normalized mean squared error (NMSE) in Figure 8 is substantial for several endpoints (especially docking scores like ESR1, F10, MET where NMSE exceeds 0.5-0.6), which may lead to missing the very best active compounds.

Limitation on non-linear molecular interactions: Combinatorial chemistry often exhibits highly non-linear structure-activity relationships (SAR) and activity cliffs. The additive factorization (Eq 12) implicitly assumes that the synthon contributions to the latent embedding can be linearly combined. It is unclear how well this holds when synthons exhibit strong cooperative or steric clash effects.

Training cost of the surrogate: The surrogate requires 1 million fully evaluated compounds (with docking scores) for training. While feasible with fast GPU-based docking, this represents a significant upfront cost that may not scale well to more expensive scoring functions (like co-folding or quantum mechanics).

Limited comparison with other state-of-the-art virtual screening baselines: The comparison is mainly against a Thompson Sampling baseline. Comparing against other surrogate-based or active learning screening methods (such as MolPal or active design space pruning) would strengthen the empirical claims.

strengths: Innovative factorization framework: Adapting additive/bilinear factorization over the combinatorial synthesis library (CSL) structure allows encoding costs to scale with the number of building blocks O(|S|) rather than the library size O(|D|).

Highly impressive speed and scale: Virtually screening a 10-billion compound library in under 30 seconds on a single Tesla T4 GPU represents a major practical advancement in high-throughput virtual screening.

Declarative and dynamic constraint handling: Unlike iterative search methods (such as RL or Bayesian Optimization), APEX supports arbitrary combinations of objectives and constraints on the fly without needing to retrain or fine-tune models.

Creation of an open benchmark: The authors constructed an open-source 10B CSL along with fully enumerated 12M and 1M subsets with docking scores, enabling exact retrieval evaluations and serving as a great contribution to the community.
Zero-shot generalization: Successful enrichment of docking scores on the real 70B Enamine REAL library demonstrates the robust generalization of the learned embeddings and factorization scheme.
weaknesses: Limitation of additive approximations: The linear factorized approximation of molecular embeddings assumed by APEX may struggle to capture non-additive, cooperative interactions between R-groups which are often critical in protein-ligand binding and 3D docking conformations.

Limited baseline comparisons: While Thompson Sampling is a suitable baseline, the empirical evaluation would be stronger by comparing against other established surrogate-based virtual screening algorithms (e.g., active learning or V-SYNTHES) under similar computational budgets on the 12M compound library.

Dependence on reaction definitions: The method heavily relies on the hierarchical structure (synthon, R-group, reaction) of CSLs, meaning it cannot easily be applied to unstructured databases of arbitrary molecules.
